text: Then she discovered six hundred and three records of her driving.
Its OnStar system logged things like hard braking, acceleration, and speeding.
That data could be turned into reports used by insurance companies.
So your price could change even without a ticket.
And this wasn't just one complaint.
The FTC accused General Motors and OnStar of collecting and selling sensitive driving data without proper consent.
In 2026, regulators finalized a five-year ban on sharing certain driving data with consumer reporting agencies.
Would you trust a car that keeps a file on your driving?
